Volume 10 · Chapter 06

Options and binomial replication

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v10-c05

By the endConstruct replicating portfolios and price options through state-contingent payoffs.

Build the payoff, finance the hedge, and respect the exercise clock

Capability. Replicate European option payoffs with signed stock and cash positions, derive the binomial pricing probabilities, construct a self-financing multi-date hedge, and prove and apply finite-date optimal exercise. The prerequisite is forwards, futures and swaps. We also use the finite positive-state-price logic of arbitrage and discount factors and conditional expectation from probability. There is no assumed Black–Scholes formula or stochastic calculus.

Linden Treasury wants protection against a fall in an asset while keeping its gains if the price rises. A forward fixes an exchange obligation; a put gives a right to sell at a chosen strike. That right has a nonlinear payoff and, when exercise is allowed early, a decision attached to it. Pricing requires more than predicting an average asset price. We must identify an attainable portfolio that pays the same amount in each modeled state, and finance its changes without hidden cash injections.

All examples are original synthetic CU-denominated contracts. Stock trades, fractional holdings and signed cash positions are available without default, taxes, bid/ask spreads or transaction costs, except in the explicitly named fee intervention. Borrowing and lending use the same specified gross return. Exercise and settlement are immediate at the stated model dates. Those assumptions define a conditional teaching market; they do not describe every option or guarantee an executable real-world hedge.

1. Rights, payoffs and financed profit

A call gives its holder the right to buy one unit at strike K; a put gives the right to sell one unit at K. Write x+ = max(x,0). With terminal underlying price ST, the European call payoff is (ST − K)+ and the European put payoff is (K − ST)+. A short option has the negative of the holder's payoff. For a physically settled contract, the cash expressions assume the acquired or delivered asset is simultaneously traded at the same specified spot price. Contract multipliers scale both premium and settlement cash.

“European” means exercise only at the specified maturity, not a geographical location. “American” means exercise is permitted before maturity as well. Our finite market permits decisions only at its modeled dates; the lab's name american_grid makes that restriction explicit. These are exact prices for that exercise grid. They are not automatically exact prices for a contract exercisable at every instant in a continuous market. A specified subset of exercise dates is often called Bermudan; adding opportunities cannot reduce the holder's value, but between-date dynamics need their own model.

The current intrinsic payoff is (St − K)+ for a call or (K − St)+ for a put. It is cash that could be obtained by exercising now if that right is available. It is not necessarily the value of a European option before maturity. Nor is the payoff the investor's profit. If a premium c is financed at gross return BT/B0, terminal net cash from holding a European call is its payoff minus cBT/B0. An investor paying from cash instead has an opportunity-cost comparison that must specify the alternative investment.

A long call and a long put have limited nonnegative exercise payoffs, but their financed net returns can be negative. A writer receives a premium while taking contingent obligations. The maximum loss of a short put on a nonnegative asset is bounded by strike before premium/funding adjustments; a call writer facing an unbounded underlying price does not have that same bound. Our finite tree has bounded terminal states by construction, which must not be mistaken for a universal cap on market exposure.

2. European parity and order restrictions

For the same asset, strike K, maturity T and cash/credit/settlement terms, compare two portfolios at T: a call plus K CU of cash, and a put plus one asset. If ST ≥ K, both are worth ST; if ST < K, both are worth K. With no interim payout, no arbitrage therefore gives c + KD(0,T) = p + S0. For known cash dividends with PV I and an attainable prepaid terminal stock, replace S0 by A = S0 − I. The dividend strips belong to the stockholder, not automatically to the option holder.

c − p = A − KD(0,T) = D(0,T)[F(0,T) − K].
max(0,A − KD) ≤ c ≤ A;   max(0,KD − A) ≤ p ≤ KD.

The bounds assume K ≥ 0, a nonnegative terminal asset and positive pricing of attainable claims. They follow from payoff inequalities: a call lies between zero and ST and exceeds ST − K; a put lies between zero and K and exceeds K − ST. A lower bound on c need not be its present intrinsic payoff: dividends or negative interest can change the comparison. For American contracts the holder can exercise at different times, so European parity is not generally an equality for their quoted prices.

European calls are decreasing and convex in strike under a fixed positive pricing rule. For K1 < K2, their terminal payoff difference lies in [0,K2 − K1], so 0 ≤ c(K1) − c(K2) ≤ (K2 − K1)D. The function K ↦ (ST − K)+ is convex in every state; multiplying its defining convex inequality by positive state prices and summing proves price convexity. These are comparisons among contracts with identical remaining terms, not permission to combine different maturities or collateral arrangements without adjustment.

The options section of Haugh's 2016 introductory notes provides further reading on parity and finite stock/cash replication. Here the payout entitlement, nonnegative-asset assumption and exercise clock are explicit. None of our numerical examples is taken from those notes.

3. Solve two cash equations before introducing a probability

At a node the stock costs S > 0. Next period it will be uS or dS, with 0 < d < u, and both branches have positive physical probability. One CU in the cash account becomes R > 0 CU. A portfolio consists of Δ shares and b CU in the account now; b < 0 means borrowing. To reproduce next-period claim values Hu and Hd, solve

ΔuS + Rb = Hu,   ΔdS + Rb = Hd.
Δ = (Hu − Hd)/[S(u − d)],   b = (uHd − dHu)/[R(u − d)].
V = ΔS + b = [qHu + (1 − q)Hd]/R,   q = (R − d)/(u − d).

The determinant S R(u − d) is nonzero, so the hedge exists and is unique for any pair of finite cash payoffs. This is a complete one-period market: the two traded payoff vectors span both states. The price follows from the portfolio cost. If the claim were more expensive, sell it and buy the replica; if cheaper, buy it and reverse the replica. The terminal obligations cancel in both states. This argument requires the permitted signed stock and cash positions and matched settlement rights.

No-arbitrage condition. With both distinct branches possible, the condition is d < R < u. If R ≤ d, borrow S and buy a share: terminal wealth is S(u − R) or S(d − R), nonnegative and positive in at least one possible state. If R ≥ u, short a share and lend S: wealth is S(R − u) or S(R − d), again an arbitrage. Equality at either endpoint is included; it does not remove the profitable other branch. If d < R < u, then q and 1 − q are strictly positive. For any portfolio, its initial value equals the positive weighted discounted sum of its two future payoffs. A portfolio with nonnegative future cash and positive cash in at least one state must therefore have positive initial cost. Neither a free positive payoff nor an initial receipt with no future liability is possible. This proves both directions.

The numbers q and 1 − q are the pricing probabilities. State prices are q/R and (1 − q)/R. Under this law, EQ[Snext] = RS, so discounted stock is a martingale. Nothing required the physical up probability p to equal q or investors to be indifferent to risk. Holding S, u, d and R fixed while changing p does not change the replicating cash equations. Changing beliefs in an actual market may also change those observable/model inputs; the conditional result does not claim beliefs never affect prices.

If u = d = R, the stock and cash payoff vectors are collinear; the two-state hedge formulas have a zero denominator. A payoff that differs between the nominal branches cannot be spanned by those assets. If a physical branch is impossible, remove it and analyze the resulting market rather than use a fictitious positive-support theorem. Clipping an invalid q to [0,1] silently changes the pricing model and does not repair an arbitrage in the supplied asset/cash terms.

Worked example 1 — The stock and loan replicate the option

Linden's stock costs 80. In one period it becomes 100 or 60, so u = 5/4 and d = 3/4. Cash gross return is R = 21/20 = 1.05; strike is 82. The call pays 18 or 0. Thus Δ = 18/40 = 9/20 and b = −(9/20)60/1.05 = −180/7. The portfolio costs 36 − 180/7 = 72/7 ≈ 10.285714 CU. At the up node it pays 45 − 27 = 18; at the down node 27 − 27 = 0.

The put pays 0 or 22. Its hedge is Δ = −11/20 and b = 1100/21, costing 176/21 ≈ 8.380952. At the up node −55 + 55 = 0; at the down node −33 + 55 = 22. The pricing probability is q = (1.05 − 0.75)/(1.25 − 0.75) = 3/5, and averaging either payoff with that q and discounting reproduces the hedge cost.

Parity checks c − p = 40/21 = 80 − 82/1.05. If the same call could be sold for 11, buying its replica and writing the call yields 11 − 72/7 = 5/7 CU now with zero terminal net cash. The claim of arbitrage refers to these executable rights. A different physical up frequency does not alter that state-by-state cancellation.

4. Multi-period replication is financed rebalancing

Let dates be i = 0,…,n. In the homogeneous tree Si,j = S0ujdi−j, where j counts up moves. A stock-price recombination does not mean all claims depend only on j: a path-dependent payoff needs the additional relevant history in its state. For a European payoff H at date n, set Vn = H and work backwards using the two successor values in the one-step hedge formula. At every node compute Δi, bi and Vi = ΔiSi + bi.

At the next node the inherited portfolio is worth ΔiSi+1 + Rbi, exactly Vi+1 by its two-state construction. The new portfolio also costs Vi+1. Hence the cash needed to change the number of shares is supplied by the change in the cash account:

(Δi+1 − Δi)Si+1 + bi+1 − Rbi = 0.

This is self-financing. It asserts zero external cash at rebalancing, not a constant number of shares, zero borrowing or zero risk before the claim is included. Induction now proves that the initial portfolio pays H on every full path: the inherited value always buys the next node's replica, and the last step buys the specified payoff. It also proves completeness for any finite-history terminal claim in the fully branching stock/cash tree when the state includes that history.

Repeated conditional expectation gives V0 = EQ[H]/Rn for this constant-R model. The probability of a particular path with j up moves is qj(1 − q)n−j. If H depends only on terminal stock, sum those paths using the binomial coefficient. For general node-specific rates or probabilities, use conditional products and dated discounting rather than substitute one unconditional frequency. The finite self-financing and martingale framework is developed further in Haugh's discrete-time pricing notes.

Worked example 2 — Follow the loan through both first moves

Keep S0 = 80, u = 5/4, d = 3/4, R = 21/20 and K = 82, but allow two periods. Terminal stocks are 45, 75 and 125; the call pays 0, 0 and 43. At the date-1 down node S = 60 both future call payoffs vanish, so its value and hedge are zero. At the up node S = 100 the call value is q·43/R = 172/7, with Δ = 43/50 and b = −430/7.

At date 0, Δ = (172/7 − 0)/(100 − 60) = 43/70, b = −1720/49, and c = 688/49 ≈ 14.040816. The terminal expectation independently gives (3/5)²·43/(21/20)² = 688/49.

After an up move, inherited stock is worth (43/70)100 = 430/7 and inherited debt is (1720/49)(21/20) = 258/7. Wealth is 172/7. Increasing shares to 43/50 requires (43/50 − 43/70)100 = 172/7 CU. Debt grows from 258/7 to 430/7, financing exactly that purchase. At the final up or down node the portfolio is (43/50)125 − 64.5 = 43 or (43/50)75 − 64.5 = 0.

After a first down move, selling the inherited 43/70 shares at 60 produces 258/7, exactly enough to repay the inherited debt. The remaining portfolio is zero and both subsequent paths are covered. “Update delta” is incomplete unless this accompanying cash-account change is shown. The European put value is 3712/441 ≈ 8.417234, so c − p = 2480/441 = 80 − 82/R², an independent terminal-parity check.

5. Early exercise is a decision based on current information

Let Hi be the nonnegative cash received on exercise at date i. An exercise time τ is a stopping time when the decision whether τ = i uses only observations available by i. In a tree, two paths sharing the same node history must make the same exercise decision there. One cannot exercise at date 1 on the path that will later fall and continue at that same date-1 history on the path that will later rise unless the future branch is already observable.

Define Vn = Hn. Working backwards, let Ci be the cost of replicating the next node's option values, and set

Ci = [qVi+1,u + (1 − q)Vi+1,d]/R.
Vi = max(Hi, Ci).

Optimality proof. At the last date exercise gives exactly Hn. Suppose V at date i + 1 is the best value over all feasible future stopping rules. A holder at date i either exercises now for Hi, or waits one period and can then choose the best rule separately at either observed successor. The latter choice has value Ci by conditional valuation; no other information is available. Taking the larger value establishes the recursion by induction. Selecting exercise when H > C and continuing when H ≤ C, with exercise/settlement at n, constructs a feasible maximizing rule. Ties may instead be exercised without changing value.

There is a useful verification interpretation. Discounted Vi/Ri exceeds discounted H and has conditional expected next value at most its current value, so it is a supermartingale. For any bounded stopping time τ, repeatedly condition one step at a time on whether exercise has occurred; this gives EQ[Vτ/Rτ] ≤ V0. Since Hτ ≤ Vτ, every feasible stopping rule has value at most V0. Along the constructed rule, all pre-exercise nodes have V = C, so those inequalities are equalities, and at exercise H = V. Thus

V0 = maxτ adapted, 0≤τ≤n EQ[Hτ/Rτ].

The optional-stopping argument here uses only a bounded horizon, finite states and iterated expectation; no unproved infinite-horizon sampling theorem is being invoked. The maximum is over exercise policies that respect information, not independent choices of the largest realized payoff on every completed path.

Why this is also the no-arbitrage option price. A writer starting with V can cover every exercise decision: at a node V ≥ H covers exercise; if the holder continues, invest C in the next-value replica and retain V − C ≥ 0 in cash. Positive cash returns preserve any retained surplus. Repeating gives a superhedge without external injections. Selling above V and using this strategy yields an initial surplus while covering the holder's rights. Conversely, if the option costs less than V, buy it, commit to the maximizing stopping rule, and sell the self-financing stock/cash strategy replicating that rule's stopped payment. On its continuation nodes V = C, so the strategy needs no surplus consumption; at its exercise date it pays exactly H. The stopped payments cancel, leaving an initial gain. These two arguments prove uniqueness in this complete, frictionless finite market. They do not prove unique prices for arbitrary incompletely spanned early-exercise claims.

Worked example 3 — A put can be worth exercising before maturity

In the two-period Linden tree, a strike-82 put pays 37, 7 and 0 at the terminal stock nodes 45, 75 and 125. At the date-1 down node S = 60, continuation is [(3/5)7 + (2/5)37]/1.05 = 380/21 ≈ 18.095238. Immediate exercise pays 22, so exercise is better. At the up node S = 100, immediate payoff is zero but continuation is [(2/5)7]/1.05 = 8/3, so continue.

At the root continuation is [(2/5)22 + (3/5)(8/3)]/1.05 = 208/21 ≈ 9.904762, exceeding immediate payoff 2. Thus the finite-grid put is worth 208/21, versus European value 3712/441. The early-exercise premium is 656/441 ≈ 1.487528. The root writer hedge is Δ = −29/60, b = 340/7: after the down move it is worth −29 + 51 = 22; after the up move it is worth −145/3 + 51 = 8/3.

If a holder unexpectedly continues after the down move, the writer has 22 while the continuation hedge costs only 380/21. The extra 82/21 can stay in cash. This explains why a writer's superhedge need not consume all initial premium for every suboptimal holder policy. Under the optimal policy, paths beginning D stop at date 1 and receive 22; UD receives 7 at date 2; UU receives zero. Discounting with their Q probabilities gives (2/5)22/R + (3/5)(2/5)7/R² = 208/21.

A hindsight calculation is different. On DD it would wait for 37/R², on DU it would take 22/R, on UD it would wait for 7/R², and on UU it would exercise at the root for 2. Its apparent value is 139378/11025 ≈ 12.641995. The root cannot know that UU will occur, and the date-1 down node cannot distinguish DD from DU yet. This number values extra future information, not the permitted put.

6. The early-exercise conclusions depend on rates and dividends

For a non-dividend-paying stock with R ≥ 1 at each step and K ≥ 0, waiting to maturity is at least as valuable as exercising a call now. In the homogeneous model, at a node with m periods left its European value satisfies cE ≥ max(0,S − K/Rm) ≥ (S − K)+. The first inequality follows from payoff dominance and discounted stock pricing; the second uses Rm ≥ 1. Backwards induction then makes the early-exercise recursion equal to the European value at every node: the continuation value is already at least immediate exercise. The American-grid and European call prices coincide.

This is a weak dominance statement. A worthless call or a zero-rate case can have ties; “early exercise is never strictly better” is more precise than claiming every early exercise is strictly irrational. If R > 1, K > 0 and current intrinsic payoff is positive, the retained financing value gives a strict inequality in this model. For a put, receiving K earlier can be valuable, as Worked example 3 shows. The statement CA ≥ CE or PA ≥ PE follows from the inclusion of terminal exercise among the allowed choices, regardless of whether early exercise actually helps.

Worked example 4 — Two ways to invalidate the non-dividend, nonnegative-rate conclusion

Negative rate. S = 100, K = 80, u = 1.1, d = 0.9 and R = 0.98. This is arbitrage-free because 0.9 < 0.98 < 1.1. Pricing q is 0.4, and the terminal call pays 30 or 10. Its European value is [0.4(30) + 0.6(10)]/0.98 = 900/49 ≈ 18.367347. Immediate exercise gives 20, so a call exercisable now or at the next date is worth 20. Its continuation hedge is one share with borrowing 4000/49. Delaying payment of the strike has a different financing effect when the cash account shrinks.

Known dividend and an explicit grid. Now S = 100, K = 80, R = 1.02. At the next date the stock pays a known dividend 12 immediately before ex-dividend settlement, when its price is 100 or 70. Stockholders receive total gains 112 or 82. Assume exercise is possible only now or after that dividend; there is no extra pre-dividend exercise date. A pricing rule must satisfy 102 = q(112) + (1 − q)82, so q = 2/3. The call's terminal payoff is 20 or 0, giving European value 2000/153 ≈ 13.071895. Immediate exercise pays 20 and is optimal on this two-date exercise grid.

The dividend-case call hedge is Δ = 2/3, b = −8200/153. At the up node its stock plus dividend is (2/3)112, and its cash debt is (8200/153)(1.02), leaving 20; at the down node the same calculation leaves zero. The put value is 500/153, and c − p = 1500/153 = 100 − (12 + 80)/1.02. Ignoring the stock's dividend when deriving q instead gives (102 − 70)/(100 − 70) = 16/15, which is not a probability. Clipping it would conceal the missing entitlement. Adding a later pre-dividend exercise opportunity is a different option and requires additional stock-price information; this example does not claim to solve it.

7. Hedge errors reveal which assumption changed

Backward induction can produce an exact number while the implementation is wrong. Check both successor payoffs of every node hedge, not only the root price. Record inherited stock, accumulated cash, stock-trade cash and the new bank balance. Check that physical probabilities affect scenario frequencies without entering the replication values when other inputs remain fixed. For early exercise, compare stopping decisions at nodes sharing the same history; any dependence on a later branch is look-ahead information.

A rebalancing fee changes the funded wealth equation. It does not disappear because the original delta was correct in a costless model. If the old strategy is followed while a fee is debited from cash, its later shortfall is the fee plus the subsequent financing effect. This is an intervention on an existing strategy, not a derivation of an optimal policy or unique option price in a market with transaction costs. Additional cash, a changed hedge, less frequent trading, or price bounds may be appropriate under a newly specified frictional model.

Worked example 5 — An ideal hedge ceases to be self-financing at its old premium

Use the two-period call hedge in Worked example 2 and charge 1% of the absolute stock-trade cash only at the interior date. There is no opening, closing or cash-account fee. After a first up move the stock purchase is 172/7, so the fee is 43/175 ≈ 0.245714. After a first down move the liquidation trade has magnitude 258/7, so the fee is 129/350 ≈ 0.368571. Borrow those fees, keep the ideal subsequent stock holdings, and do not inject external cash.

At the final date the shortfalls are (43/175)(21/20) = 129/500 = 0.258 on both paths starting U, and (129/350)(21/20) = 387/1000 = 0.387 on both paths starting D. Costless hedge errors remain exactly zero; the changed funded strategy has these negative errors. It is insufficient to compare only the aggregate option payoff with an endpoint stock gain. The lab reports both ledgers so the failure can be traced to the interior payment.

Reproducible finite-options laboratory

Download the original Linden inputs, standard-library Python model, full exact reference output, contract and run instructions, and integrity manifest. The preserved model computes all call/put, European/grid-exercise nodes, statewise replication residuals, every full-path hedge ledger, optimal stopping receipts and the two exercise counterexamples. It uses fractions rather than floating-point equality tests.

The declared domain is one to six periods with strictly interior pricing probabilities and bounded positive inputs; this is sufficient for exhaustive transparent checks, not large production valuation. Rejecting R at a branch boundary is intentional. Predict the effect of changing only physical_up, only interior_rebalance_fee, and the strike before comparing outputs. The first changes physical scenario weights, the second changes the intervention ledger, and the third changes contractual payoffs and exercise decisions. No input is a market observation.

Exercises

State the position, dates, units and exercise rights. Exercises 2, 7 and 8 require proofs; numerical checks do not substitute for those arguments. Exercise 10 is an open research/model critique with explicit criteria.

  1. New two-state claim. S = 62, next stock prices are 80 and 50, R = 1.04 and K = 64. Find both call and put payoffs, their stock/cash replicas, pricing q and prices. Check parity. If the call premium is borrowed at R, compute its terminal net cash in both states. Explain why the nonnegative call payoff does not imply nonnegative financed profit.
  2. Necessary and sufficient trading conditions. Prove d < R < u is necessary and sufficient in the one-step model with both branches physically possible. Give explicit arbitrage cash for S = 70, u = 1.2, d = 1 and R = 0.98. Explain the endpoint R = d = 1 and the different degenerate case u = d = R. State why q clipping is not a valid repair.
  3. Dividend-adjusted parity trade. S = 50, a known dividend of 2 is paid at date 0.5 with discount 0.99, maturity is 1 with discount 0.96 and strike is 52. The otherwise matched European call and put quote 4 and 5. Determine the parity discrepancy and give an explicit initial, dividend-date and maturity portfolio exploiting it under the chapter's reversible-trading assumptions.
  4. A new two-period hedge. S0 = 60, u = 4/3, d = 2/3, R = 1, K = 61 and n = 2. Compute the terminal call payoffs, date-1 values, root price and every stock/cash position. Verify self-financing after each possible first move and terminal replication on all four paths. Find the European put price by terminal expectation and check parity.
  5. Exercise-policy transfer. Change the two-period Linden put's strike to 88, leaving S0 = 80, u = 5/4, d = 3/4 and R = 21/20. Compute terminal put payoffs, both date-1 continuation values, exercise decisions, root finite-grid value, European value and early-exercise premium. Describe the information available to the exercise rule. Does selecting the largest discounted receipt separately on each completed path solve the same problem?
  6. Physical probabilities. In the original strike-82 two-period Linden tree, change the physical up probability from 0.7 to 0.25 while holding stock branches, prices and R fixed. Find the discounted physical expected call payoff and compare it with the replication price. Which parts of the stock/cash hedge and Q stopping values change? Explain why a difference in expected return is not a statewise arbitrage.
  7. Exercise theorem and boundaries. Prove that in the non-dividend homogeneous tree with R ≥ 1 and K ≥ 0, the finite-grid call equals its European counterpart. Explain possible ties. Use the negative-rate parameters S = 100, K = 80, u = 1.1, d = 0.9, R = 0.98 to identify precisely which inequality fails. Prove that enlarging the set of permitted exercise dates cannot reduce holder value when the underlying market and information model are otherwise unchanged.
  8. Strike convexity audit. Derive monotonicity, the vertical-spread bound and convexity for matched European call prices as functions of strike. A dealer's same-maturity calls at strikes 70, 80 and 90 quote 18, 14 and 8. Construct the equally spaced butterfly payoff and evaluate its initial cost. Give its payoff on each of the four stock-price intervals and explain the arbitrage under executable matched terms, even though the three prices decrease with strike.
  9. Funded fee reserve. For Worked example 5, independently compute both interior stock trade sizes, fees and terminal shortfalls. Find the smallest deterministic amount of extra cash placed in the bank at date 0 that covers both shortfalls while leaving the original stock strategy unchanged. Show the terminal residual on each first-move branch. State why this is not a proof of the minimum possible option-writing cost in a fully specified market with transaction costs.
  10. Model and research critique. A report prices a finite-grid put using historical up frequencies, chooses its exercise date with the benefit of each simulated full future path, replaces negative pricing weights by zero and renormalizes, and reports its costless delta hedge as a guaranteed market hedge despite observed trading fees. Design a corrected pricing and validation protocol. Use at least one scoped primary reading, a quantitative counterexample from this chapter and a feasible out-of-sample check. Identify the data and trading assumptions required before interpreting a refined tree as a real contract price.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. Replica cost and the investor's financed result

    The call pays (16,0) and the put (0,14), ordering states up/down. q = (1.04·62 − 50)/30 = 181/375, with down weight 194/375. Call Δ = 16/30 = 8/15; b = −(8/15)50/1.04 = −1000/39. Its price is (8/15)62 − 1000/39 = 1448/195 ≈ 7.425641. The up cash is (8/15)80 − (1000/39)(1.04) = 16 and down cash is zero.

    Put Δ = −14/30 = −7/15; b = [(7/15)80]/1.04 = 1400/39. Price is −(7/15)62 + 1400/39 = 1358/195 ≈ 6.964103. The two resulting payoffs are 0 and 14. Parity gives c − p = 6/13 = 62 − 64/1.04. A loan financing the call premium requires repayment (1448/195)(1.04) = 2896/375. Terminal net cash is therefore 3104/375 ≈ 8.277333 up and −2896/375 ≈ −7.722667 down. Paying for the right is part of the investment cash flow.

  2. Positive state prices rule out both forms of arbitrage

    If R ≤ d, buy one stock financed by borrowing S; next cash is S(u − R), S(d − R), both nonnegative and at least one positive. If R ≥ u, short the stock and lend S; next cash is S(R − u), S(R − d), with the same property. For d < R < u, q/R and (1 − q)/R are positive and price both the stock and the account. Their linear combination prices every portfolio. A nonnegative, nonzero payoff vector must have positive price, contradicting any nonpositive-cost arbitrage; a zero payoff cannot have negative price. This establishes sufficiency and necessity with positive physical support.

    For the stated numbers, borrow 70, buy one stock, and repay 68.6 next period. Future stocks are 84 and 70, so net cash is 15.4 or 1.4 with zero initial cost. At R = d = 1, cash is 14 or 0; the up branch still has positive probability, so equality remains an arbitrage. If u = d = R instead, stock duplicates cash and gives no such spread; the two instruments have rank one. A branch-specific payoff cannot generally be hedged, and the division by u − d is undefined. Clipping a noninterior q changes the valuation weights without making the supplied traded cash vectors consistent with strictly positive state prices.

  3. The dividend strip must be repaid on its actual date

    I = 2(0.99) = 1.98 and A = 50 − 1.98 = 48.02. Required c − p = 48.02 − 52(0.96) = −1.90; the quotes give −1, an excess of 0.90 CU. Call plus a 52-CU maturity bond costs 4 + 49.92 = 53.92. Put plus prepaid terminal stock costs 5 + 48.02 = 53.02. Sell the first portfolio and buy the second.

    Explicitly, write the call (+4 now), borrow 52 due at maturity (+49.92 now), buy the put (−5), buy the stock (−50), and borrow 2 due at the dividend date (+1.98). Initial net receipt is 0.90. The dividend of 2 repays the interim loan. At maturity, stock plus put minus call is always 52, repaying the maturity borrowing. Every later net cash is zero. This proof needs the stated dividend entitlement, both option directions, stock borrowing where needed for reversals, matched settlement and access to the quoted funding.

  4. The cash account makes the changing delta affordable

    q = (1 − 2/3)/(4/3 − 2/3) = 1/2. Date-1 stocks are 40 and 80; terminal stocks are 80/3, 160/3 and 320/3. Call payoffs are 0,0,137/3. The date-1 down value is zero with zero holdings. At the up node the value is 137/6, Δ = (137/3)/(160/3) = 137/160 and b = −137/3.

    Root value is 137/12; Δ = (137/6)/40 = 137/240 and b = −137/6. After an up move inherited wealth is (137/240)80 − 137/6 = 137/6. The new stock purchase costs (137/160 − 137/240)80 = 137/6, financed by additional borrowing of exactly 137/6. At UU the final portfolio pays (137/160)(320/3) − 137/3 = 137/3; at UD it pays zero. After a first down move, selling the inherited shares gives (137/240)40 = 137/6, repaying all debt; DD and DU then both pay zero.

    Terminal put payoffs are 103/3, 23/3 and 0, with probabilities 1/4,1/2,1/4. Put price is 149/12. Difference c − p = −1 = 60 − 61, matching R = 1. All calculations concern the same two-period model; no continuous limit is needed.

  5. Choose at the node, not after the last branch

    Terminal put payoffs are 43,13,0. At S = 60, continuation is [(2/5)43 + (3/5)13]/(21/20) = 500/21 ≈ 23.809524; immediate exercise is 28, so exercise. At S = 100, continuation is [(2/5)13]/(21/20) = 104/21 ≈ 4.952381, exceeding immediate zero, so continue.

    Root continuation is [(2/5)28 + (3/5)(104/21)]/(21/20) = 1984/147 ≈ 13.496599, which exceeds intrinsic 8. The European value is [(4/25)43 + (12/25)13]/(21/20)² = 5248/441 ≈ 11.900227. Early-exercise premium is 704/441 ≈ 1.596372. The policy uses the observed first move and current stock; it does not know the second move when making the date-1 choice. Selecting the best date separately after seeing every full path permits distinctions between identical date-1 histories and can also let the root anticipate its eventual path. It solves a problem with more information. Worked example 3 supplies an explicit overvaluation of that type.

  6. A conditional replication price does not change with a frequency input alone

    Only UU has positive terminal call payoff, equal to 43. At physical p = 0.25, EP[H]/R² = 43(1/4)²/(21/20)² = 1075/441 ≈ 2.437642. The replication price remains 688/49 ≈ 14.040816, because q remains 3/5 and the traded payoff equations are unchanged. Every ideal hedge holding, both-branch replication residual, Q price and Q-optimal stopping value is unchanged. Physical path weights and physical expected receipts change.

    A position can have an unattractive or attractive physical mean return while losing in some states. The two state prices still value its attainable cash, and no zero-cost nonnegative payoff is created merely by relabeling physical frequencies. In a real calibration, revised information may alter S, branch sizes, funding or trading access as well; then the conditional no-change calculation would no longer describe the same inputs.

  7. Weak dominance, not an unconditional exercise slogan

    With m periods left, terminal call payoff is nonnegative and at least ST − K. Its discounted price is therefore at least max(0,S − K/Rm). Because R ≥ 1 and K ≥ 0, this is at least (S − K)+. At the penultimate date, continuation for the grid call is the European continuation and exceeds immediate exercise. Inductively, if the two successor grid values equal European values, their continuation is again the European value and again dominates immediate exercise. Thus equality of grid and European prices holds at every node. A zero-payoff region or R = 1 may give equality, so early exercise can tie without increasing value.

    At R = 0.98, R−1 > 1, and S − K/R = 100 − 80/0.98 = 900/49 is less than S − K = 20. That is the failed rate comparison. Both terminal call payoffs are positive, so their European value equals this lower amount, and immediate exercise strictly improves it.

    For exercise sets E ⊆ E′ within the same underlying probability/information market, every E-admissible stopping rule is also E′-admissible. The maximum discounted payoff expectation over E′ is therefore at least that over E. This does not compare two trees with different branch processes, calibrations or information. Refining the exercise grid while also changing the market model needs a separate convergence argument.

  8. A decreasing price list can still violate convexity

    For K1 < K2, 0 ≤ (ST − K1)+ − (ST − K2)+ ≤ K2 − K1 in every state. Positive valuation gives the monotonicity and discounted vertical-spread bound. Convexity follows by applying positive valuation to the statewise convex inequality for K ↦ (ST − K)+. For equally spaced strikes it requires c(70) − 2c(80) + c(90) ≥ 0.

    Buy one strike-70 call, write two strike-80 calls and buy one strike-90 call. Quoted cost is 18 − 28 + 8 = −2 CU: receive 2 now. Its terminal payoff is zero for ST ≤ 70; ST − 70 for 70 ≤ ST ≤ 80; 90 − ST for 80 ≤ ST ≤ 90; and zero for ST ≥ 90. It is nonnegative everywhere. The initial receipt with no later negative cash is an arbitrage under matched executable terms, regardless of whether the interior triangle has positive probability in a particular tree. Bid/ask quotes, sizes, fees or unmatched terms must be used before applying this conclusion to market data.

  9. A reserve for a fixed strategy is not an optimal frictional price

    Initial Δ is 43/70. Up-node Δ becomes 43/50, so the purchase costs (43/50 − 43/70)100 = 172/7; down-node Δ becomes zero, so the sale magnitude is (43/70)60 = 258/7. Multiplying by 1% gives fees 43/175 and 129/350. Funding for one further period multiplies by 21/20, producing terminal errors −129/500 and −387/1000.

    An extra deterministic bank amount x at date 0 grows to xR². To cover both errors it must satisfy xR² ≥ max(129/500,387/1000) = 387/1000. The least such x is (387/1000)/(21/20)² = 86/245 ≈ 0.351020408 CU. Its terminal residual after fee coverage is 0.129 CU on either U-first path and zero on either D-first path. The added position is cash only, so it does not alter the named stock-trade fee under this intervention.

    This minimum is over deterministic extra bank reserves for the fixed ideal stock strategy and fee schedule. It does not optimize stock trading, exercise/hedging jointly, bid/ask execution or a general nonlinear cost model. A different strategy could change both the cash exposure and the fees themselves. No universal transaction-cost option price has been proved.

  10. Separate the model, the policy and its validation sample

    Start from an executable market and an explicit contract. Record spot and strike units, payment and exercise dates, dividend entitlement, stock-borrow rights, cash borrowing/lending rates, spreads and fees. In the frictionless two-branch benchmark, derive q from the stock and cash payoff equations and require 0 < q < 1. Use historical probabilities for scenario frequency or empirical estimation, not as an automatic substitute for the replication rule. Exercise 6 shows a discounted physical mean of 1075/441 while the same cash-replication price remains 688/49. If supplied branches violate the no-arbitrage inequality, diagnose rates, payouts or calibration; do not clip q and pretend the same assets are priced.

    Compute early exercise using current-node information and backward continuation values. Freeze a candidate policy before evaluating it on new paths; a policy optimized using a path's later outcomes has extra information. The original put's hindsight value 139378/11025 exceeds its feasible value 208/21 because it makes incompatible decisions at common histories. In simulation-based extensions, keep training, policy selection and out-of-sample policy evaluation separate, and report simulation and approximation error. A finite exercise grid represents only its declared opportunities until a convergence argument justifies a refinement limit.

    Audit all nodewise hedge payoffs and all rebalance cash. The fee example gives shortfalls of 0.258 or 0.387 even with exact ideal deltas. Reconcile a frozen hedge rule against later observed settlements using actual tradable bid/ask prices, fees, dividends and funding dates, rather than only fitted terminal prices. Compare independent implementations and stress a payout misclassification, boundary q, missing exercise date and funding/fee increase. Use Haugh's scoped discrete-time treatment as the primary methodological reference for self-financing and information-adapted exercise; it does not validate a selected real instrument's inputs.

    Evaluation. Full credit requires repairing all four report errors; a correct quantitative example; explicit exercise information and trading assumptions; a feasible independent or out-of-sample validation design; and a distinction between model consistency, numerical convergence and empirical fit. A finer tree alone cannot prove its payoff model, trading access or cost assumptions correct. No claim of a guaranteed hedge is justified by a root-price match or a backtest that selects exercise after seeing the future.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain why the binomial price does not start by asking how often the stock rises, and why a correct delta alone is not a complete dynamic hedge.

Model answer. Two stock/cash equations match the claim's two possible receipts, and their initial portfolio cost fixes its no-arbitrage price under the stated trading rights. The pricing weight q is then derived from stock and cash prices; the physical frequency p describes a different quantity. At the next node delta changes, and the accompanying bank-account change must finance the stock trade without an external deposit. For an early-exercise claim the hedge must also cover the holder's permitted current-information decision, not a future-informed policy.

Delayed retention, after 7–14 days. (i) S = 50, u = 1.2, d = 0.8, R = 1 and K = 52: find q, call Δ, cash b and price. (ii) At an exercise node immediate payoff is 12 and discounted continuation is 10.5: find option value and the writer's cash surplus if the holder continues. (iii) State which assumption fails if a stock paying a dividend is priced by a stock-only ex-dividend martingale. (iv) Explain why three completed paths can share an exercise decision even if their later optimal-in-hindsight dates differ.

Answers. (i) q = 1/2, payoffs are 8 and 0, Δ = 0.4, b = −16 and price 4. (ii) Value is 12; the writer can buy the continuation hedge for 10.5 and retain 1.5, though the holder should exercise if maximizing this model value. (iii) The traded stock's total gain includes the dividend; discounted ex-dividend price alone need not be a martingale. (iv) Until their histories diverge, a feasible stopping rule sees the same information and must make the same decision. Advancement requires these answers and a fresh two-step hedge with every rebalance cash reconciled.

Sources and extensions

Haugh, Forwards, Swaps, Futures and Options (2016), Section 4, and Haugh, Martingale Pricing Theory in Discrete-Time and Discrete-Space Models (2016), self-financing and American-option sections, are the primary further-study routes. Our finite proofs, Linden data, exercises and implementation are original. We use weak early-exercise dominance with explicit rate and dividend assumptions; source statements are not extended beyond those conditions.

Continuous trading, Brownian uncertainty and limits of increasingly fine trees require additional probability and convergence arguments. Brownian motion and Itô calculus supplies the next tools, followed by Black–Scholes valuation. Incompleteness, jumps, stochastic volatility and transaction costs can break exact replication or change the relevant price bounds. The discrete analysis remains useful precisely because each payoff, information restriction and financing requirement is visible.

Sources and further study

  • Martin Haugh — Forwards, Swaps, Futures and Options (2016) — Section 4: European parity, payoff bounds, two-state replication and multi-period stock/cash valuation. All Linden examples and problems are original.
  • Martin Haugh — Martingale Pricing Theory in Discrete-Time and Discrete-Space Models (2016) — Finite self-financing stock/cash strategies, conditional martingale valuation and American exercise backward recursion. The chapter supplies its own bounded finite proof and original numerical cases.
